other_side: Zitron's answer to "you have a capability overhang" is that the overhang is a story told by people who need you to keep buying. In his account the tech industry has become a cargo cult, "people doing impressions of things that have worked before", and AI adoption is the purest example: executives who do not do the work mandate the tools because someone they admire said to. He is blunt about the demand side too, arguing the popularity of AI "has come entirely from social pressure and endlessly-discounted access", and that the moment real prices arrived customers started asking about ROI. He reads the industry's sudden enthusiasm for agentic loops as a revenue mechanism rather than a discovery, noting that Anthropic's Claude Code lead is allowed to burn upwards of a hundred and thirty thousand dollars a month in tokens, and saying flatly that it is unclear what benefits a loop might have.
truth_beneath: The variable both men circle is the gap between what AI can be shown doing and what it can be shown paying for. Both accept the demos are real: Zitron never disputes that a model checked Mollick's 195 references, he disputes that such anecdotes aggregate into economics. The empirical question that will resolve is whether skilled agentic use survives unsubsidised pricing, and the observable is renewal and seat-expansion on full-price agent tiers once free credits stop. The residue is pure worldview: whether slow uptake is a learning curve or a polite name for not worth the money. NLW is vindicated if heavy users keep paying real prices and firms show margin gains; Zitron is vindicated if usage falls away when the discounts do. Both are polemicists with skin in the game: NLW is launching a training programme premised on your overhang, Zitron sells subscriptions premised on certain collapse. Where they agree is the signal, and both say executives mandating AI they do not understand is a genuine failure mode. Watch full-price retention.
